analysis.one_liner: Makes the reduced individual tax rates on capital gains and dividends permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently extend the 2003 cuts to capital gains and dividend tax rates, sponsored by one senator with six Republican cosponsors, never received a committee vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Bush tax law cut the tax rate on capital gains (profits from selling investments) and lowered the tax on stock dividends for individuals, but included a built-in expiration date so those cuts would lapse [S2]. This bill would delete that expiration date, making the lower rates on investment income permanent with no end [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never taken up [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment income. Capital gains and dividend income are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest taxpayers, so making the reduced rates permanent delivers its largest dollar benefits to them. Public corporations and the financial industry also benefit, since a permanently low dividend tax makes stocks more attractive and lowers the cost of raising capital.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the termination date in the 2003 Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act covering the reduced individual capital gains rates and the taxation of dividends at capital gain rates, so those reductions would no longer lapse [S2] [S3].

Capital gains and dividend income are concentrated in the highest-income households, so permanent extension of the reduced rates delivers its largest benefits to investors who hold substantial stock portfolios.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Making the rates permanent is an unpaid-for tax cut: it permanently forgoes revenue whenever investors realize gains and receive dividends, which must be made up through other taxes, spending cuts, or borrowing.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal Treasury and other taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the sunset with no offsetting revenue provision, making the lost revenue permanent rather than temporary [S2] [S3].

Because gains and dividends go disproportionately to high-income households, the largest tax reductions accrue to those least in need of a rate cut, and the revenue cost must be covered by other taxpayers or borrowing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow heavily to the top of the income distribution while its cost lands on the Treasury indefinitely, with no mechanism to pay for it. As a standalone permanent tax cut for investment income introduced during a deficit period, it offered little for ordinary working people, who mostly realize little or no capital gain and hold little dividend income outside retirement accounts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never received a markup or vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Crapo introduced the bill on October 4, 2011, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5] [S1].
Six Republican senators signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and no vote on it ever occurred before the Congress ended [S5].
Because the bill never passed, the scheduled expiration of the reduced capital gains and dividend rates remained in place, leaving that revenue available unless future legislation extended the rates.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the expiration date on the reduced investment-income rates stood, preserving federal revenue and leaving the rates' future to later negotiations rather than locking them in permanently. Wealthy investors gained nothing from this particular bill, though the broader fate of the rates was later decided in separate end-of-2012 negotiations rather than here.

for.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the reduced capital gains and dividend rates permanent.

for.name: Six Republican senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Republican — one sponsor and six Republican cosponsors, no Democrats — though the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record of opposition exists.

industries.industry: Wealthy households with capital gains and dividend income
industries.note: Making the reduced rates permanent would permanently lower taxes on income that flows mainly to the top of the income distribution, with the cost borne by the Treasury. Their gain comes directly from revenue other taxpayers must eventually cover.

industries.industry: U.S. public corporations and the financial industry
industries.note: A permanently low tax on dividends makes stock investments more attractive, lowering the cost of equity capital for corporations and brokerages. The benefit to these industries comes at the price of foregone federal revenue.
